title: What counts as a vector?
question: What makes something a vector?
hook: Forces, polynomials and functions turn out to follow the very same rules.
idea: A vector is any element of a set that can be added and scaled by numbers under the vector axioms.

beats.prompt: Two students pick different bases for the same vector space. The first finds that her basis has three vectors. How many vectors does the second find in his?

choices.label: Any number, since the two bases are different
choices.feedback: Different bases are allowed, but all bases of one vector space have the same size.

choices.label: More than three, because a basis can always grow
choices.feedback: Adding a vector to a basis would break independence; every basis has the same size, which is the dimension.

beats.explain: All bases of a vector space have the same cardinality, called the dimension of the space.

beats.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Non-empty subset closed under adding and scaling
The set of all linear combinations of some elements
Linearly independent elements that span the space
The common size of every basis
beats.explain: These four ideas build on each other: subsets that stay inside the space, what a set generates, the smallest generating sets, and their size.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which one?
steps: A vector space is a set whose elements can be added together and scaled.
The elements of any such set are called vectors.
So every vector must be an arrow with a magnitude and a direction.
So a set of polynomials could never be a vector space.
beats.explain: Vector spaces generalize Euclidean vectors, and polynomial rings are themselves vector spaces, so vectors need not be arrows.

beats.prompt: Two vector spaces over the same field both have the same dimension. What can you say about them?

choices.label: They are isomorphic, so structure-only properties match exactly
They contain exactly the same vectors
choices.feedback: Same dimension does not mean same elements; one could hold arrows and the other polynomials.

choices.label: They both describe physical forces
choices.feedback: Vector spaces are far more general than forces and velocities.

choices.label: They must both be infinite-dimensional
choices.feedback: A dimension can be a natural number, which makes the space finite-dimensional.

beats.explain: For two vector spaces over a given field with the same dimension, the properties that depend only on the vector-space structure are exactly the same.
